answer:
Split the question, because the three things you want to capture do not all sit on the same side of the line.

(1) THE DISPOSAL-REVIEW DECISION IS DOCUMENTED HISTORY, AND IT MODELS CLEANLY. A review is a past act of appraisal, carried out by a named officer on a named date, that ends in a verdict about the file. That is exactly E17 Type Assignment: P41 classified -> the case file, P42 assigned -> an E55 Type ('retain permanently' / 'approved for destruction'), P14 carried out by -> the records officer, P4 has time-span -> the date of the review. E17's scope note is written for this situation: it covers classification acts 'in cases where the value of the classification depends on the personal opinion of the classifier, and the date that the classification was made'. The spec's 'Authorship of Knowledge Base Contents' section confirms the intent - statements of responsibility in the CRM are expressed through E13 Attribute Assignment and its subclasses, so a curator's appraisal is attributed to that curator rather than absorbed silently into the institution's own voice. Successive reviews of the same file give you successive instances of E17, which is what you want: the file's appraisal history, not just its current status. If for some files you only need the verdict and not who or when, P2 has type on the file is the CRM's declared shortcut for exactly that path (full path: E1 -> P41i was classified by -> E17 -> P42 assigned -> E55).

(2) THE GROUND FOR RETENTION IS A PROPERTY OF THE DECISION, NOT OF THE FILE. Record it on the E17, not on the file, because the same file can be retained for a statutory reason at one review and a curatorial one at the next. Use P21 had general purpose -> E55 Type, with two terms from your own vocabulary ('statutory retention requirement' vs 'historical importance'); where there is an actual instrument, add P17 was motivated by -> the statute (P17 is defined as 'an item or items that are regarded as a reason for carrying out' the activity), which lets you say which statute rather than only that there was one. Do not reach for E30 Right for the statutory case: E30 is scoped to legal privileges such as reproduction and property rights, and a statutory duty to retain is an obligation on the authority rather than a privilege over the file; E30 also has nowhere to hang the officer or the date.

(3) THE RETENTION SCHEDULE, AS THE PROCEDURE THAT WAS FOLLOWED, IS ALSO IN SCOPE. Model it as E29 Design or Procedure - 'documented plans for the execution of actions' that shape or guide the execution of an activity; its own examples include the ISO standardisation procedure. Attach it with P33 used specific technique (E7 -> E29), which is the only CRM property that takes a procedure as the thing an activity was carried out under. That records the true and useful fact that this review was conducted under the fifteen-year planning-application schedule, and it survives revision of the schedule, since each review points at the version it actually used.

(4) THE NEXT REVIEW DATE IS WHERE IT STOPS BEING DOCUMENTED HISTORY. A due date is not a fact about the past; it is a trigger in a workflow. The CRM has deliberately refused this ground three times over. On the list, Christian-Emil Ore's objection to the original Activity Plan proposal was flat: the CRM is retrospective and does not talk about the future. The SIG then resolved Issue 166 by ruling future events out - dealing with future instances of E4 is a matter for extensions and 'not part of the scope of CRM'. Issue 333 moved the plan model into CRMsoc, and Issue 419 finally made it a stand-alone extension, CRMact, precisely because it is the 'only model that is future oriented'. Independently of all that, the spec's own Intended Scope draws the line where your case sits: exchange of information with archives is explicitly inside it, but 'Information required solely for the administration and management of cultural institutions' - the paradigm cases given are personnel, accounting and visitor statistics - is outside it. A tickler queue of files falling due is administration in that sense.

So: yes, a different kind of system - but only for the forward-looking part. Keep the retention schedule as an operative rule and the next-review dates in the records management system (or an EDRMS following ISO 15489 / a preservation-metadata system), which is what is actually built to fire on a date. Write into the CRM the completed acts: who decided what about which file, when, under which schedule, and on which ground.

IF YOU MUST PUBLISH THE DATE ANYWAY, publish it as a documented assertion, not as a scheduled event. An E13 Attribute Assignment made at the last review, with P140 assigned attribute to -> the file, P177 assigned property of type -> an E55 Type 'next disposal review due', and P141 assigned -> an E52 Time-Span, states the retrospective and true fact that somebody set a date. E52's scope note licenses this reading: instances of E52 may be defined 'representing a declaration of a temporal extent, as, for instance, done in a business contract' - a declarative rather than phenomenal time-span, whose value you pin with P170 defines time from an E61 Time Primitive. What you have not done is assert that a future event exists, and no CRM consumer will treat the date as a commitment.

One thing I deliberately left out: E6 Destruction. When a file is actually destroyed that is squarely documented history and E6 is the class, but P13 destroyed ranges over E18 Physical Thing, so it will not carry a born-digital case file without an extension, and the case asks about the decision rather than its execution.

rejected_alternatives.why_not: Scoped to 'legal privileges concerning material and immaterial things ... reproduction and property rights'. A statutory duty to retain is an obligation borne by the authority, not a privilege held over the file, and E30's property set has no place for the reviewing officer or the review date, so it cannot carry the decision either.

Tempting because a disposal review is collection care, but its necessary property P147 curated ranges over E78 Curated Holding, i.e. the aggregation, not an individual file, and E87 gives no way to record what was decided. It is the right class for the review programme as a whole, not for the per-file verdict.

rejected_alternatives.option: E6 Destruction for the disposal outcome
rejected_alternatives.why_not: Correct for a physical file that is actually destroyed, but it models the execution, not the decision or the schedule, and P13 destroyed ranges over E18 Physical Thing, so it does not reach a born-digital case file.

rejected_alternatives.option: A CRMsoc / CRMact Activity Plan for the retention schedule and due date
rejected_alternatives.why_not: This is where the SIG did put forward-looking constructs (Issue 333 to CRMsoc, Issue 419 to the stand-alone CRMact), so it is the honest pointer - but it is outside CRMbase by design, and the archive here holds no scope note or property list for those classes (SO1 comes back with no definition on file), so I cannot responsibly specify a mapping against them.

rejected_alternatives.option: Putting the review date on the file with P4 has time-span, as if a future review were an event
rejected_alternatives.why_not: P4 attaches a time-span to an E2 Temporal Entity that actually happened. A review that has not occurred is not an instance of E2, and Issue 166 closed exactly this door for future instances of E4.

rejected_alternatives.option: E32 Authority Document for the retention schedule
rejected_alternatives.why_not: E32 covers encyclopaedias, thesauri and authority lists - reference works that list entities. A retention schedule prescribes actions; it is not a controlled vocabulary.

siblings_considered.why_not: E14 Condition Assessment is the other E13 subclass that documents an expert's opinion about a holding, but it assesses state of preservation and its P35 has identified points at an E3 Condition State. A disposal review judges evidential and historical value against a schedule, not physical condition; recording 'retain permanently' as a condition state would be a category error.

E87 Curation Activity is the sibling under E7 that a records manager would reach for first, but it is anchored to an E78 Curated Holding by its necessary P147 and carries no assigned value. Setting a next-review date is an assertion about one file, which is what E13 with P177/P140/P141 exists to express.

E31 Document is the nearest sibling under E73 and the schedule is of course also a document, but E31 comprises items that 'make propositions about reality' - descriptive - whereas a retention schedule is prescriptive, and only E29 is in the range of P33 used specific technique, which is the link that says the review was conducted under it. Nothing stops the same thing being typed both ways; E29 is what licenses the modelling.

E89 Propositional Object would let you model 'the statutory requirement' as a full proposition or rule, which is more faithful to a statute but useless for the query the case needs - sorting files by the ground of retention. E55 is defined as concepts denoted by terms from thesauri and controlled vocabularies, and it is what P42 and P21 take as range.

E2 Temporal Entity, the sibling under E1, comprises phenomena that happen over an extent of time. A review that has not happened is not a phenomenon, so it cannot be an instance of E2; E52 is the purely abstract extent, and its scope note explicitly admits declarative time-spans that state a temporal extent rather than observe one.

notes: Two things the tools made awkward. First, the CRMsoc/CRMact side of the answer is reachable only through the issue register and the minutes: 'concept SO1' returns a CRMsoc identifier with no scope note on file, and 'concept "Activity Plan"' finds nothing, so I could name the extension the SIG created but could not inspect its classes or properties and deliberately did not map anything onto them. Second, issue pages are searchable but their chunk ids are not printed by the human-readable 'issues' output; I had to re-run 'docs --kind issue --json' to get 'issue166#current-s0000' before 'quote' would accept it - plain 'quote 166' and 'quote issue:166' both fail with 'unknown source id'. Same for spec chunks: '--json' was the only way to see 'crm732#s0005' and to read a narrative chunk in full rather than as a 300-character preview. One residual judgement call: I read the case's 'next review date' as a live workflow trigger. If it is instead a historical field on closed files ('the date this file was next due when the 2009 review ran'), it is uncontroversially past fact and the E13/E52 assertion pattern is not a fallback but the right answer.
